summary.title: Give me /events, not webhooks
summary.one_liner: Webhooks leave two systems prone to eventual inconsistency, so exposing a cursor-based /events endpoint that consumers poll (ideally with long-polling) gives stronger consistency guarantees.
takeaways: Webhooks alone cannot keep two systems consistent; their delivery guarantees are loose and events are ephemeral, so they are hard to replay after bugs or outages.
A /events endpoint with a locally stored cursor lets a consumer catch up at its own pace and rewind to replay events after a bug fix.
Postgres replication slots and Stripe's /events endpoint are used as models: a changelog plus a per-consumer cursor, with full entity payloads embedded in each event.
Polling /events is more work on the consumer side but avoids a message bus; long-polling could reduce the cost of frequent empty polls.
Webhooks remain fine for low-stakes notifications; polling /events is preferred when consistency matters.
summary.summary: The article argues that webhooks are a weak basis for keeping services in sync: they are ephemeral, hard to replay, and need extra infrastructure like message buses and HMAC signing, and they still require polling in practice. It proposes an /events endpoint modeled on Postgres replication slots and Stripe's events API, where the consumer keeps a cursor and polls for changes. The author lists benefits such as recovery at the consumer's pace, replay by rewinding the cursor, and reuse of existing API code, and suggests long-polling to reduce empty requests. It closes by advising when each approach fits and how producers can build events tables that also support webhooks.
